media.instructions_for_student: The student measures the sides of a triangle, folds it to compare its angles, and names it equilateral, isosceles or scalene, seeing that equal sides go with equal angles.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Triangle Check
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S10.T10.C45.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity (measure, fold and sort triangles)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Triangles from the Rhombus: the rhombus divided into four triangular pieces, questions 1 to 3 and the "Try This" folding questions on isosceles, equilateral and scalene triangles (developer only). Each piece measures 4 cm, 7 cm and 8 cm (the middle side is about 6.9 cm and is shown as 7 cm). Practice values: card triangles of 9, 9, 5 cm and 10, 8, 6 cm and 7, 7, 7 cm.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student measures the sides of a triangle, folds it to compare its angles, and names it equilateral, isosceles or scalene, seeing that equal sides go with equal angles.
- Out of scope: measuring angles with an instrument, other triangle names, any rule about the sum of angles.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A light-wood workbench seen from above. A big card triangle (sides 9, 9 and 5 cm, drawn so that 1 cm is 20 pixels) lies in the middle and is the largest thing on the stage. A wooden ruler lies across the top edge. Three shallow wooden trays stand along the bottom edge, labelled "Equilateral", "Isosceles" and "Scalene".
- Instruction line: "Measure the sides of the triangle with the ruler."
- The ruler pulses once, inviting the child to drag it onto a side.
2. Scene and Objects
- Triangles: card cut-outs with a soft shadow and a round dot on each corner. Practice triangles P1 (9, 9, 5 cm), P2 (10, 8, 6 cm) and P3 (7, 7, 7 cm), and the 4 blue pieces of the rhombus, each with sides 4, 7 and 8 cm.
- Ruler: drag it onto a side or tap a side; it slides along and a tag shows the length to the nearest whole cm. Side list: three boxes under the bench; two boxes with the same number glow green with an equals sign.
- Fold: tap a corner (it glows orange), then "Fold". The triangle folds along the line from that corner to the middle of the opposite side. A line says "The halves match" or "The halves do not match"; corners that land on each other get matching green arcs. "Unfold" opens it.
- Halve button (Star Challenge 7 only): cuts along that line and slides the halves apart so the ruler can measure each.
- Join bench (Star Challenges 1, 4 and 5): the 4 blue pieces lie on the bench. A piece snaps to another only whole side to whole side with the same length. "Turn" turns the chosen piece half way round, "Flip" flips it. The tool names the shape made; "Trace" copies it into a gallery of 6 small cards.
- Tray counter "sorted 2 of 3"; goal chip such as "3 sides". Bottom buttons (three only): Hint, Reset, Next (locked until the chip is green).
3. Main Interaction
- Measure by dragging or tapping, fold by choosing a corner then Fold, sort by dragging a triangle into a tray. A tray takes a triangle only after all 3 sides are measured and a fold has been tried. Reset clears trays, side list and gallery.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Measure all 3 sides of triangle P1. How many sides are equal?" Goal chip: "3 sides". Setup: P1 (9, 9, 5 cm). Help: guided, the sides are tagged "side 1" to "side 3". Guess: number cards 0, 2 and 3. Result: the list reads 9, 9 and 5; the two 9 boxes glow green. Why line: "9 cm and 9 cm are equal, and 5 cm is different, so 2 sides are equal."
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Fold P1 so that the two halves lie on each other." Goal chip: "Fold". Help: guided, corners named "top", "left" and "right". Guess: the child taps the corner they think will match. Result: only the fold from the corner between the two 9 cm sides matches; the corners at the ends of the 5 cm side land on each other. Why line: "The halves match from the corner between the two 9 cm sides, so the two angles at the ends of the 5 cm side are equal."
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Measure and fold P2 and P3, then put all three triangles in the right trays." Goal chip: "Sort 3". Setup: P1, P2 and P3. Guess: before measuring P3, number cards 1, 2 and 3 for how many folds will match. Result: P2 (10, 8, 6) has no equal sides and no fold matches: Scalene. P3 (7, 7, 7): every fold matches: Equilateral. P1: Isosceles. Why line: "P3 has 3 equal sides and 3 folds match; P1 has 2 and 1; P2 has none and none." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "What geometrical shapes can you make by fitting 2 of these triangles together? Trace the shapes you created." Goal chip: "Trace 4 shapes". Setup: the join bench. Guess: "I think I can make:" cards "2 shapes", "4 shapes" and "6 shapes". The child joins pairs and traces; the goal is 4 different shapes. Result: the tool shows all 6: 2 triangles, a kite, a rectangle and 2 parallelograms. Why line: "2 pieces make 2 triangles and 4 four-sided shapes: 2 + 4 = 6 shapes." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "How many different types of triangles can you make? Now, observe and measure the sides of these triangles. What do you notice?" Goal chip: "Types". Setup: the 2 triangles of Star Challenge 1 as cards. Guess: cards 1, 2 and 3. The child measures both. Result: 2 types: sides 8, 8 and 8, and a wider one with sides 8, 8 and 14. Why line: "Both triangles have 2 equal sides, and in the first one all 3 sides are equal." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "Trace the isosceles triangles on a paper and cut them out. Fold them in half. What do you notice about their angles?" Goal chip: "Fold". Setup: the wider triangle (8, 8, 14 cm). Guess: "The two angles at the ends of the third side will:" cards "match" and "not match". Result: folded from the top corner, the halves match. Why line: "The two halves match, so the two angles at the ends of the third side are equal: an isosceles triangle has 2 equal angles." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line: "Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are equal (equilateral triangle)?" Goal chip: "Equilateral". Setup: the join bench, cleared. Guess: cards "Yes" and "No". The child joins 2 pieces along their 7 cm sides with one flipped, and measures. Result: Yes. Why line: "The two long sides are 8 cm each, and the two short sides lie in a straight line: 4 + 4 = 8 cm, so all 3 sides are 8 cm." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 5. Goal line: "Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are unequal?" Goal chip: "Scalene". Setup: the join bench, cleared. Guess: cards "Yes" and "No". Result: Yes: one piece alone has sides 4, 7 and 8 cm. Why line: "One piece has 3 different sides, so it is a scalene triangle." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 6. Goal line: "Take an equilateral triangle. Check if all the angles of an equilateral triangle are equal, just like you did with the isosceles triangle." Goal chip: "3 folds". Setup: the card triangle 8, 8, 8 cm. Guess: number cards 1, 2 and 3 for how many folds will match. The child folds from each corner. Result: all 3 match. Why line: "Every fold matches, so all 3 angles of an equilateral triangle are equal." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 7. Goal line: "Now, cut the equilateral triangle in half. How many sides of each new triangle are equal?" Goal chip: "Halve". Setup: the 8, 8, 8 triangle and the Halve button. Guess: number cards 0, 2 and 3. The child halves it and measures each half. Result: each half has sides 4, 7 and 8 cm. Why line: "No two sides of a half are equal, so each half is a scalene triangle." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 8. Goal line: "Check in scalene triangles whether any two or more angles are equal?" Goal chip: "Scalene angles". Setup: one blue piece (4, 7, 8 cm). Guess: cards "Yes" and "No". The child folds from all 3 corners. Result: no fold matches. Why line: "No fold matches, so no 2 angles are equal." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Measuring and folding, the child sees that the number of equal sides and the number of equal angles go together: 3 and 3, 2 and 2, none and none.
- Rules in the child's words: "3 equal sides: equilateral. 2 equal sides: isosceles. No equal sides: scalene." "If the halves match when I fold, the angles that land on each other are equal."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Wrong answer: red strip, a small shake of the object, and one friendly line naming the mistake and what to look at; no scores, retry is free. Correct: arcs and boxes turn green, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks.
- Fold does not match -> "The halves do not match from this corner. Try another corner." The corner pulses.
- Thinks only the sides of an isosceles triangle are equal -> "Fold it. Do the two corners land on each other?" The matching corners pulse.
- Counts a side twice or misses one -> "Measure all 3 sides first." The unmeasured side pulses.
- Wrong tray -> "Count the equal sides in your list." The equal boxes pulse and the triangle slides back.
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "How many sides of this triangle are the same length?" (2) Visual clue: the ruler slides onto the next unmeasured side. (3) Almost the answer: the tool measures all 3 sides and shows them; the child says how many are equal.
- Edge cases: the ruler rounds to whole cm, so the 7 cm side is a rounded reading; the long side of the wider triangle reads 14 cm, not equal to 8 cm; a triangle with 3 equal sides also has 2 equal sides and is called equilateral.
7. Ending
- A star challenge is done when its result in section 4 is reached; the end screen follows when all chips are green.
- End screen: confetti once. "Well done!" Remember: "3 equal sides: equilateral. 2 equal sides: isosceles. No equal sides: scalene." "Equal sides go with equal angles." "Fold a triangle to compare its angles." Think and talk: "Can a triangle have 2 equal sides and 3 equal angles?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: light-wood workbench top view (photo); card triangles in orange, yellow and green, 4 blue pieces, a wooden ruler, scissors and trays (photo cut-outs). Fold lines and arcs are code-drawn. No people. English only.

content.text:
1. Predict first: triangle A has sides 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm. Triangle B has sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm. Triangle C has sides 8 cm, 8 cm and 3 cm. Which one has all 3 angles equal, and which one has no equal angles?

4. C has 2 equal sides, so C is an isosceles triangle with 2 equal angles.
5. You can compare the angles of any shape by folding paper: angles that land exactly on each other are equal.
6. Rule: 3 equal sides means equilateral, 2 equal sides means isosceles and no equal sides means scalene; equal sides go with equal angles.

content.text:
Worked example: Triangle A has sides 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm. Triangle B has sides 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm. Triangle C has sides 8 cm, 8 cm and 3 cm. Name each triangle and say how many of its angles are equal.
1. Triangle A: the sides are 6 cm, 6 cm and 6 cm. All 3 sides are equal, so A is an equilateral triangle.
2. Fold A in half through a corner, so that the two halves lie on each other. They match through every corner, so all 3 angles of A are equal.
3. Triangle B: the sides are 7 cm, 5 cm and 4 cm. No two sides are equal, so B is a scalene triangle.
4. Fold B in half through each of its corners. The two halves never lie exactly on each other, so no two angles of B are equal.
5. Triangle C: the sides are 8 cm, 8 cm and 3 cm. Two sides are equal, so C is an isosceles triangle with 2 equal angles.
6. Check: A has 3 equal sides and 3 equal angles, C has 2 and 2, and B has none and none. The number of equal sides and the number of equal angles always match.
Answer: A is equilateral (3 equal sides, 3 equal angles), B is scalene (no equal sides, no equal angles), C is isosceles (2 equal sides, 2 equal angles)

media.teaching_notes: 1. Each piece is a triangle with 1 right angle and 3 different sides: a shortest side, a middle side and a longest side. The longest side is twice the shortest side. 2. Join 2 pieces side to side. They can meet along their shortest sides, their middle sides or their longest sides, and the second piece can be flipped over or turned half way round. 3. Along the middle sides, with one piece flipped over: a triangle with all 3 sides equal. 4. Along the shortest sides, with one piece flipped over: a wider triangle with 2 equal sides. 5. Along the longest sides, with one piece flipped over: a kite. With one piece turned half way round: a rectangle. 6. Along the middle sides or along the shortest sides, with one piece turned half way round: 2 different parallelograms that are not rectangles. 7. Check: 2 triangles and 4 four-sided shapes make 2 + 4 = 6 shapes, and each one has 3 or 4 sides. Answer: Sample answer: 2 triangles (one with 3 equal sides, one wider with 2 equal sides), a kite, a rectangle and 2 parallelograms that are not rectangles. Your answer may differ.

content.text: What geometrical shapes can you make by fitting $2$ of these triangles together? Trace the shapes you created.
content.q_figure: A rhombus divided by its two diagonals into four triangular pieces.

content.book_number: Triangles from the Rhombus: two pieces together
content.question_tex: What geometrical shapes can you make by fitting $2$ of these triangles together? Trace the shapes you created.
content.publication_text: What geometrical shapes can you make by fitting $2$ of these triangles together? Trace the shapes you created.

content.text:
1. Each piece is a triangle with $1$ right angle and $3$ different sides: a shortest side, a middle side and a longest side. The longest side is twice the shortest side.
2. Join $2$ pieces side to side. They can meet along their shortest sides, their middle sides or their longest sides, and the second piece can be flipped over or turned half way round.
[Image: Triangles from the Rhombus: Ans1: solution]
3. Along the middle sides, with one piece flipped over: a triangle with all $3$ sides equal.
4. Along the shortest sides, with one piece flipped over: a wider triangle with $2$ equal sides.
5. Along the longest sides, with one piece flipped over: a kite. With one piece turned half way round: a rectangle.
6. Along the middle sides or along the shortest sides, with one piece turned half way round: $2$ different parallelograms that are not rectangles.
7. Check: $2$ triangles and $4$ four-sided shapes make $2 + 4 = 6$ shapes, and each one has $3$ or $4$ sides.
Answer: Sample answer: $2$ triangles (one with $3$ equal sides, one wider with $2$ equal sides), a kite, a rectangle and $2$ parallelograms that are not rectangles. Your answer may differ.
[Image: Triangles from the Rhombus: Ans1: solution (continued)]

Answer: The two halves match when folded, so the two angles at the ends of the third side are equal. Each isosceles triangle has $2$ equal angles.

content.publication_text: Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are equal (equilateral triangle)?

content.text:
1. We want a triangle with $3$ sides of the same length.
2. Join $2$ pieces along their middle sides, with one piece flipped over.
3. The longest sides of the $2$ pieces become $2$ sides of the new triangle. They are equal.
[Image: Triangles from the Rhombus: Ans4: solution]
4. The $2$ shortest sides of the pieces lie in one straight line and make the third side. The shortest side is half the longest side, so $2$ shortest sides are as long as $1$ longest side.
5. So all $3$ sides are equal: an equilateral triangle.
6. Check: measure the $3$ sides with a ruler. They are the same.
Answer: Yes. Join $2$ pieces along their middle sides, with one piece flipped over. All $3$ sides are equal, so it is an equilateral triangle.

content.question_tex: Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are unequal?
content.publication_text: Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are unequal?

content.text:
1. One piece is already a triangle. Its $3$ sides are a shortest side, a middle side and a longest side, and they are all different.
2. So a single piece is a triangle with all $3$ sides unequal.
3. Bigger ones are possible too. Join the wider triangle ($2$ pieces) and $1$ more piece, longest side against one of the $2$ equal sides, and flip the piece until the outside has only $3$ sides. The $3$ sides are all different.
[Image: Triangles from the Rhombus: Ans5: solution]
4. A triangle with all $3$ sides unequal is called a scalene triangle.
5. Check: a single piece has $3$ different sides, so the answer is yes.
Answer: Yes. A single piece has $3$ different sides, and $3$ pieces can also make a bigger triangle with $3$ different sides. It is a scalene triangle.

A piece snaps whole side to whole side when one of its sides is brought near a side of the same length on another piece, with a soft click, and the joined sides turn into a dashed line inside the shape. Trace saves the shape to the tracing sheet and the gallery. Count lights each outside edge in orange one after the other while the side counter counts up. Name opens a label card with the names triangle, kite, parallelogram, rectangle, pentagon and hexagon to pick from. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Hint, Retry (separates the last piece), Reset (returns the 4 pieces to the rhombus), Undo, Back and Next are in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the number of pieces used (1 to 4), the live side counter for the outside of the shape (for example Sides: 4), the name label, the number of shapes in the gallery, and the card number out of 7. On the last card the six shape names each get Yes and No buttons.
feedback: When 2 sides touch whole side to whole side the pieces snap with a soft click, and the joined sides turn into a dashed line inside the shape. The tool says: Two sides are joined inside, so the outside has 4 sides.
Count lights each outside edge in orange one by one and the side counter counts up. Sides that line up in one straight line count as one side.
A piece brought near a side of a different length does not snap and wobbles gently with the note: These sides are not the same length. Try another side or turn the piece.
A name that does not fit the shape shows a soft amber note with a clue about sides or angles, for example: Are the equal sides next to each other or opposite each other?

On the book's cards the tool says what the shape has, for example: Your shape uses 3 pieces and has 5 sides. On the last card a Yes for a shape that has not been traced from all 4 pieces gets the note: Show it with all 4 pieces first. A wrong answer shows a soft amber note and never a red cross.

challenges: Card 1: join 2 pieces along their longest sides, with one piece flipped over. Trace it and count its sides. Answer: a kite with 4 sides. Side 1 = side 2 and side 3 = side 4, so the equal sides are adjacent.

Card 2: join 2 pieces along their middle sides, with one piece turned half way round. Trace it and count its sides. Answer: a parallelogram with 4 sides. Its opposite sides are equal and none of its corners is a right angle, so it is not a rectangle.
Card 3: join 2 pieces along their longest sides, with one piece turned half way round. Trace it and count its sides. Answer: a rectangle with 4 sides and 4 right angles. Its opposite sides are equal.

Card 4: join 2 pieces along their middle sides, with one piece flipped over. Count the sides. Answer: 3 sides, not 4. The 2 shortest sides lie in one straight line and make one side. All 3 sides are equal: it is a triangle.

Card 5: use 3 pieces. Take the triangle from card 4 and join 1 more piece, its longest side against a side of the triangle. How many sides does the shape have? Answer: 4 sides, because 3 − 1 + 2 = 4: the joined side hides inside and the new piece adds 2 sides.

Challenge: 'Using 3 triangular pieces of the rhombus, try creating a (a) 3-sided shape, (b) 4-sided shape, and (c) 5-sided shape.' Build each one, trace it and read its sides. Answer: all three can be made. (a): join the wider triangle (2 pieces joined along their shortest sides) and 1 more piece, its longest side against one of the 2 equal sides, and flip the piece until the outside has 3 sides. (b): join the triangle with 3 equal sides and 1 more piece along a longest side, and the outside has 4 sides. (c): join 2 pieces along their shortest sides with one turned half way round, put the third piece with its longest side against one of the 2 long sides, and flip it until the outside has 5 sides. In all, 3 pieces make 13 different shapes, so your shapes may differ.

Challenge: 'Which of these shapes can be made with all 4 pieces? Try and find out. (a) Square (b) Rectangle (c) Triangle (d) Pentagon (5-sided) (e) Hexagon (6-sided) (f) Octagon (8-sided)' Try each one, then press Yes or No for each name. Answer: a rectangle, a triangle, a pentagon and a hexagon can be made. A square and an octagon cannot: each piece adds at most 1 side, so 4 pieces make at most 3 + 3 = 6 sides, and no four-sided shape made of 4 pieces has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles.

media.instructions_for_student: The student joins triangular pieces whole side to whole side, counts the sides round the outside, and names kites, parallelograms and rectangles by their sides and angles.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Rhombus Pieces
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S13.T13.C64.2D1
- Tool type: Concept-activity (join pieces, count sides, name four-sided shapes)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Triangles from the Rhombus and Four-Sided Shapes: questions 4 to 8 (shapes from 2, 3 and 4 pieces, quadrilaterals A and B, kites and parallelograms on a grid) and "Make your own kite shape" by folding (developer only). Each piece has sides 4, 7 and 8 cm and one right angle.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student joins 2, 3 and 4 triangular pieces whole side to whole side, counts the sides round the outside, and names kites, parallelograms and rectangles by their sides and angles.
- Out of scope: measuring angles, other four-sided shape names, anything about how much space a shape covers.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A light table (a milky glass panel glowing softly, seen from above) with a sheet of tracing paper on it. In the middle lie the 4 triangular pieces of a rhombus, large blue card cut-outs, each with a small square mark on its right angle: the largest things on the stage. Under the table a gallery strip has 6 empty frames.
- Instruction line: "Join 2 pieces along their middle sides, one flipped over. Count the sides."
2. Scene and Objects
- Pieces: 4 identical right-angled triangles with sides 4 cm (shortest), 7 cm (middle) and 8 cm (longest), in three line styles. Joined sides become a dashed line inside; the outside edge is thick.
- "Trace" copies the outline into the next gallery frame. Side counter "Sides: 4" counts only straight edges round the outside; two sides in one straight line count as one.
- Used by some cards: a ruler tag (tap a side to read its length), a corner tester (a paper right angle to drag onto a corner), a dot grid, a yellow paper square.
- On-stage round buttons: "Flip", "Trace", "Count". Goal chip. Bottom buttons (three only): Hint, Reset, Next (locked until the chip is green).
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a piece; a whole side brought near a side of another piece with the same length snaps so the two sides lie exactly on each other. A side of a different length does not snap and wobbles. "Flip" puts the chosen piece against the same side the other way round: from "flipped over" to "turned half way round", and back. "Count" lights the outside edges one by one while the counter counts up. Reset returns the 4 pieces to the rhombus.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Join 2 pieces along their middle sides, one flipped over. Count the sides." Goal chip: "Count the sides". Help: guided, the middle sides are tagged "7 cm". Guess: "How many sides will it have?" with cards 3, 4 and 6. Result: 3 sides. Why line: "2 pieces have 3 + 3 = 6 sides. The 2 joined sides hide inside: 6 − 2 = 4. The 2 short sides lie in one straight line and make 1 side: 4 − 1 = 3."
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Join 2 pieces along their longest sides, one flipped over. Count the sides and name the shape." Goal chip: "Name it". Help: guided, the longest sides are tagged "8 cm". Guess: "Is it a kite?" with cards "Yes" and "No". Result: a kite with 4 sides. Why line: "6 − 2 = 4 sides. Side 1 = side 2 and side 3 = side 4: the equal sides are next to each other, so it is a kite."
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Join 2 pieces along their middle sides, one turned half way round. What shape is it?" Goal chip: "Name it". Guess: cards "Kite", "Parallelogram" and "Rectangle". Result: a parallelogram. Why line: "Its opposite sides are equal and no corner is a right angle: a parallelogram, not a rectangle." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "How many different 4-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make?" Goal chip: "Trace 4 shapes". Guess: cards 2, 4 and 6. The child joins pairs and traces each four-sided shape. Result: 4 different shapes: a kite, a rectangle and 2 parallelograms. Why line: "A kite, a rectangle and 2 parallelograms: 1 + 1 + 2 = 4 shapes." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "Measure the sides of each of these two quadrilaterals A and B. What do you notice? Are there any pairs of sides that are equal? Which pairs are equal, adjacent or opposite?" Goal chip: "Measure". Setup: A (2 pieces joined along the middle sides, one turned half way round: sides 8, 4, 8, 4 cm going round) and B (joined along the longest sides: sides 4, 7, 4, 7). Guess: "The equal sides are:" cards "next to each other" and "opposite each other". Result: A and B each have 2 pairs of equal sides, and they are opposite. Why line: "Each equal pair is across from each other." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "What types of angles do quadrilaterals A and B have? Which angles are equal in each of the above parallelograms?" Goal chip: "Angles". Guess: "B has:" cards "no right angle", "2 right angles" and "4 right angles". The child drags the tester onto each corner (a right angle gets a green tick) and taps two corners to see if they match. Result: A has 2 corners wider than a right angle and 2 narrower, opposite angles equal; B has 4 right angles. Why line: "B is a rectangle: a parallelogram with 4 right angles." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line: "In the grid given below, draw two different kites and parallelograms each." Goal chip: "4 shapes". Setup: a dot grid of 20 by 10 squares and 4 frames labelled "Kite", "Kite", "Parallelogram", "Parallelogram". Guess: "A kite has equal sides:" cards "next to each other" and "opposite each other". The child taps 4 dots in order; the shape closes, a card names it ("Kite: side 1 = side 2 and side 3 = side 4") and it goes into the first free frame of its kind. Sample: kite (0,3), (2,0), (4,3), (2,7); parallelogram (0,0), (5,0), (7,3), (2,3). Why line: "In a kite the equal sides meet at a corner; in a parallelogram they are across." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 5. Goal line: "Now, use 3 triangles from the rhombus to form shapes. How many sides do each one of them have? Using 3 triangular pieces of the rhombus, try creating a (a) 3-sided shape, (b) 4-sided shape, and (c) 5-sided shape." Goal chips: "3-sided", "4-sided", "5-sided". Guess: "3 pieces can make at most:" cards 4 sides, 5 sides and 9 sides. The child builds and traces one of each. Result: all three can be made (13 different shapes in all: 2, 5 and 6 with 3, 4 and 5 sides). Why line: "3 pieces have 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 sides, and 4 of them hide inside, so the outside has at most 9 − 4 = 5 sides." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 6. Goal line: "Which of these shapes can be made with all 4 pieces? Try and find out. (a) Square (b) Rectangle (c) Triangle (d) Pentagon (5-sided) (e) Hexagon (6-sided) (f) Octagon (8-sided)". Goal chip: "6 names". Setup: 4 pieces and six name cards with Yes and No buttons. Guess: the child taps Yes or No on every card, then builds; a Yes is kept only after that shape is traced from all 4 pieces. Result: rectangle, triangle, pentagon and hexagon can be made; square and octagon cannot. Why line: "Each new piece adds at most 1 side, so 4 pieces make at most 3 + 3 = 6 sides: no octagon. The pieces never make 4 equal sides with 4 right angles, so no square." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 7. Goal line: "Make your own kite shape. Start with a square piece of paper. Fold one corner towards the opposite corner to make a crease along the diagonal. Open and fold corner A inwards, aligning the edge with the crease. Repeat with corner B. What shapes do you see in the kite?" Goal chip: "Fold a kite". Setup: a yellow paper square, corner A at the bottom left, corner B at the top right. Guess: "The folded shape will look like a:" cards "kite", "square" and "rectangle". The child drags A to B (a crease shows), then A inwards, then B inwards, each flap snapping when its edge lies along the crease, then taps the shapes seen: "triangles". Result: 4 triangles. Why line: "2 folded flaps and 2 triangles under them make 2 + 2 = 4 triangles." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- A joined side hides inside, sides in a straight line make one side, and each new piece adds at most 1 side.
- Rules in the child's words: "A kite has equal sides next to each other. A parallelogram has equal opposite sides." "A rectangle is a parallelogram with 4 right angles."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Wrong answer: red strip, a small shake of the object, and one friendly line naming the mistake and what to look at; no scores, retry is free. Correct: the outside edge turns green, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks.
- Counts the joined sides -> "A joined side is inside, so it is not counted." The dashed lines pulse. Counts 2 sides in a straight line as 2 -> "These 2 sides lie in one straight line, so they make 1 side." Both pulse.
- Calls a parallelogram a kite -> "Are the equal sides next to each other or opposite?" The equal pairs glow.
- Says a rectangle is not a parallelogram -> "A rectangle is a special parallelogram: its opposite sides are equal too." The opposite sides glow. Draws a shape that is neither -> "Look at the sides: which ones are equal?" The sides show their lengths.
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "Which sides must touch: the longest, the middle or the shortest?" (2) Visual clue: the two sides to join glow. (3) Almost the answer: the tool joins the pieces.
- Edge cases: 2 pieces joined along the middle sides, one flipped, make 3 sides, not 4; on the grid a rhombus or a rectangle goes in a parallelogram frame.
7. Ending
- A star challenge is done when its result in section 4 is reached; the end screen follows when all chips are green.
- End screen: confetti once. "Well done!" Remember: "A joined side hides inside, so count only the outside edges." "A kite has equal sides next to each other. A parallelogram has equal opposite sides." "A rectangle is a parallelogram with 4 right angles." Think and talk: "Why can 4 pieces never make an octagon?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: light table with tracing paper (photo); 4 blue card pieces and a yellow paper square (cut-outs). Dot grid, joins, counter and cards are code-drawn. English only.

Worked example: A four-sided shape has sides 5 cm, 5 cm, 3 cm and 3 cm going round in that order. Is it a kite? Then check a shape whose sides going round are 5 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm.

2. Side 1 and side 2 are next to each other and both are 5 cm, so side 1 = side 2. They are adjacent sides.
3. Side 3 and side 4 are next to each other and both are 3 cm, so side 3 = side 4.
4. Two pairs of adjacent sides are equal, so the shape is a kite.
5. Now the second shape: 5 cm, 3 cm, 5 cm and 3 cm. Side 1 and side 3 are both 5 cm, but they are opposite sides, not next to each other.
6. Side 2 and side 4 are both 3 cm and also opposite. Equal opposite sides make a parallelogram, so this shape is not a kite.
7. Check: both shapes have two 5 cm sides and two 3 cm sides. Only the order round the shape decides.
Answer: The first shape is a kite, because its equal sides are next to each other (side 1 = side 2 and side 3 = side 4). The second shape has equal opposite sides, so it is a parallelogram, not a kite

Quadrilaterals whose opposite sides are equal are called parallelograms.
In parallelogram A, opposite angles are equal.
In parallelogram B, all angles are equal and are right angles. Such a parallelogram is called a rectangle.
A rectangle is a special type of parallelogram.

5. So the sides alone do not tell us if a shape is a rectangle. We also need the angles.

media.teaching_notes: 1. Join 2 pieces side to side. The joined side hides inside, so 2 pieces with 3 sides each give 3 + 3 − 2 = 4 sides outside, unless two sides line up in a straight line. 2. Join along the longest sides, with one piece flipped over: a kite. 3. Join along the longest sides, with one piece turned half way round: a rectangle. 4. Join along the middle sides, with one piece turned half way round: a parallelogram that is not a rectangle. Join along the shortest sides, with one piece turned half way round: another one. 5. That is 4 different four-sided shapes: a kite, a rectangle and 2 parallelograms. Sliding a piece along a joined side makes even more, so there are at least 4. 6. Check: each of the 4 shapes has 4 sides, counted round the outside. Answer: Sample answer: at least 4: a kite, a rectangle and 2 parallelograms that are not rectangles. Your answer may differ.

media.teaching_notes: 1. Shape A has 4 sides. Its 2 long sides are each the longest side of a piece, and its 2 short sides are each the shortest side of a piece. 2. Measure: the 2 long sides are the same length, and the 2 short sides are the same length. 3. Each long side is across from the other long side. So the equal pairs of A are opposite sides, not adjacent sides. 4. Shape B has 4 sides: 2 sides are the shortest side of a piece and 2 sides are the middle side of a piece. 5. Measure: the 2 shorter sides are equal and the 2 longer sides are equal, and each equal pair is opposite. 6. Check: in A and in B the equal sides are opposite each other, so none of the equal pairs is adjacent. Answer: In both A and B there are 2 pairs of equal sides, and the equal sides are opposite each other, not adjacent.

media.teaching_notes: 1. Each piece has 3 sides, so 3 pieces have 3 + 3 + 3 = 9 sides. Joining 3 pieces takes 2 joins, and 4 of the 9 sides hide inside, so the outside has at most 9 − 4 = 5 sides. Sides that line up in a straight line make one longer side, so a shape can have fewer. 2. (a): 3-sided shape. Join the wider triangle (2 pieces joined along their shortest sides) and 1 more piece, with the longest side of the new piece against one of the 2 equal sides of the wider triangle. Flip the piece until the outside has 3 sides. It is a big triangle with 3 different sides. 3. (b): 4-sided shape. Join the triangle with 3 equal sides (2 pieces joined along their middle sides) and 1 more piece, with the longest side of the new piece against a side of the triangle. The outside has 4 sides. 4. (c): 5-sided shape. Join 2 pieces along their shortest sides, with one turned half way round, to make a slanted shape. Put the third piece with its longest side against one of the 2 long sides, and flip it until the outside has 5 sides. 5. Check: count the sides round the outside of each shape: 3, 4 and 5. In all, 3 pieces make 13 different shapes: 2 with 3 sides, 5 with 4 sides and 6 with 5 sides. Answer: Sample answer: yes. (a): a big triangle with 3 different sides. (b): the triangle with 3 equal sides and 1 more piece, 4 sides. (c): a slanted shape and 1 more piece, 5 sides. Your answer may differ.

hold_back: A rectangle, a triangle, a pentagon and a hexagon can be made. A square and an octagon cannot.

media.teaching_notes: 1. Each new piece joined along a whole side covers 1 side and adds 2 new sides, so it adds at most 1 side. 2. A piece has 3 sides, and the other 3 pieces add at most 3 more. So 4 pieces make a shape with at most 3 + 3 = 6 sides. 3. (a): no square. A square needs 4 equal sides and 4 right angles. The shape with 4 equal sides that 4 pieces make is the rhombus, which has no right angle, and the rectangles have 2 different side lengths. 4. (b): rectangle, yes. Make a rectangle from 2 pieces (longest sides together, one piece turned half way round), make a second one the same, and join the 2 rectangles along sides of the same length. 5. (c): triangle, yes. Join the triangle with 3 equal sides (2 pieces) and the wider triangle (2 pieces) along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has only 3 sides. They make a big triangle. 6. (d): pentagon, yes. Join a kite (2 pieces) and a rectangle (2 pieces) along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has 5 sides. 7. (e): hexagon, yes. Join 2 kites along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has 6 sides. 8. (f): no octagon. A shape made of 4 pieces has at most 6 sides, and an octagon has 8. 9. Check: yes for the rectangle, triangle, pentagon and hexagon, and no for the square and the octagon. Answer: A rectangle, a triangle, a pentagon and a hexagon can be made. A square and an octagon cannot.

content.text: How many different $4$-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make?
content.q_figure: A rhombus divided by its two diagonals into four triangular pieces.
content.question: How many different 4-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make?
content.book_number: Shapes from the Rhombus: four-sided shapes
content.question_tex: How many different $4$-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make?
content.publication_text: How many different $4$-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make?

content.text:
1. Join $2$ pieces side to side. The joined side hides inside, so $2$ pieces with $3$ sides each give $3 + 3 - 2 = 4$ sides outside, unless two sides line up in a straight line.
2. Join along the longest sides, with one piece flipped over: a kite.
3. Join along the longest sides, with one piece turned half way round: a rectangle.
[Image: Shapes from the Rhombus: Ans1: solution]
4. Join along the middle sides, with one piece turned half way round: a parallelogram that is not a rectangle. Join along the shortest sides, with one piece turned half way round: another one.
5. That is $4$ different four-sided shapes: a kite, a rectangle and $2$ parallelograms. Sliding a piece along a joined side makes even more, so there are at least $4$.
6. Check: each of the $4$ shapes has $4$ sides, counted round the outside.
Answer: Sample answer: at least $4$: a kite, a rectangle and $2$ parallelograms that are not rectangles. Your answer may differ.

content.text:
1. Shape $A$ has $4$ sides. Its $2$ long sides are each the longest side of a piece, and its $2$ short sides are each the shortest side of a piece.
2. Measure: the $2$ long sides are the same length, and the $2$ short sides are the same length.
3. Each long side is across from the other long side. So the equal pairs of $A$ are opposite sides, not adjacent sides.
[Image: Shapes from the Rhombus: Ans2: solution]
4. Shape $B$ has $4$ sides: $2$ sides are the shortest side of a piece and $2$ sides are the middle side of a piece.
5. Measure: the $2$ shorter sides are equal and the $2$ longer sides are equal, and each equal pair is opposite.
6. Check: in $A$ and in $B$ the equal sides are opposite each other, so none of the equal pairs is adjacent.
Answer: In both $A$ and $B$ there are $2$ pairs of equal sides, and the equal sides are opposite each other, not adjacent.

content.text:
1. Each piece has $3$ sides, so $3$ pieces have $3 + 3 + 3 = 9$ sides. Joining $3$ pieces takes $2$ joins, and $4$ of the $9$ sides hide inside, so the outside has at most $9 - 4 = 5$ sides. Sides that line up in a straight line make one longer side, so a shape can have fewer.
[Image: Shapes from the Rhombus: Ans5: solution]
2. $(a)$: $3$-sided shape. Join the wider triangle ($2$ pieces joined along their shortest sides) and $1$ more piece, with the longest side of the new piece against one of the $2$ equal sides of the wider triangle. Flip the piece until the outside has $3$ sides. It is a big triangle with $3$ different sides.
3. $(b)$: $4$-sided shape. Join the triangle with $3$ equal sides ($2$ pieces joined along their middle sides) and $1$ more piece, with the longest side of the new piece against a side of the triangle. The outside has $4$ sides.
4. $(c)$: $5$-sided shape. Join $2$ pieces along their shortest sides, with one turned half way round, to make a slanted shape. Put the third piece with its longest side against one of the $2$ long sides, and flip it until the outside has $5$ sides.
5. Check: count the sides round the outside of each shape: $3$, $4$ and $5$. In all, $3$ pieces make $13$ different shapes: $2$ with $3$ sides, $5$ with $4$ sides and $6$ with $5$ sides.
Answer: Sample answer: yes. $(a)$: a big triangle with $3$ different sides. $(b)$: the triangle with $3$ equal sides and $1$ more piece, $4$ sides. $(c)$: a slanted shape and $1$ more piece, $5$ sides. Your answer may differ.
[Image: Shapes from the Rhombus: Ans5: solution (continued)]

content.text:
1. Each new piece joined along a whole side covers $1$ side and adds $2$ new sides, so it adds at most $1$ side.
2. A piece has $3$ sides, and the other $3$ pieces add at most $3$ more. So $4$ pieces make a shape with at most $3 + 3 = 6$ sides.
[Image: Shapes from the Rhombus: Ans6: solution]
3. $(a)$: no square. A square needs $4$ equal sides and $4$ right angles. The shape with $4$ equal sides that $4$ pieces make is the rhombus, which has no right angle, and the rectangles have $2$ different side lengths.
4. $(b)$: rectangle, yes. Make a rectangle from $2$ pieces (longest sides together, one piece turned half way round), make a second one the same, and join the $2$ rectangles along sides of the same length.
5. $(c)$: triangle, yes. Join the triangle with $3$ equal sides ($2$ pieces) and the wider triangle ($2$ pieces) along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has only $3$ sides. They make a big triangle.
6. $(d)$: pentagon, yes. Join a kite ($2$ pieces) and a rectangle ($2$ pieces) along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has $5$ sides.
7. $(e)$: hexagon, yes. Join $2$ kites along sides of the same length, and turn them until the outside has $6$ sides.
8. $(f)$: no octagon. A shape made of $4$ pieces has at most $6$ sides, and an octagon has $8$.
9. Check: yes for the rectangle, triangle, pentagon and hexagon, and no for the square and the octagon.
Answer: A rectangle, a triangle, a pentagon and a hexagon can be made. A square and an octagon cannot.

media.title: Tangram Maker

tool_config.idea: Name the seven tangram pieces and make target shapes from some or all of them: sort the pieces by their number of sides, make a square from 2 small triangles, and fill outlines by turning and flipping pieces, finding that a shape can often be made in more than one way.
tool_config.title: Tangram Maker
tool_config.screen: A wooden tangram tray on the craft table, drawn as a polished 3D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. The 7 pieces lie in the tray as flat coloured pieces, large and clear: 2 large triangles, 1 medium triangle, 2 small triangles, a square and a parallelogram. An outline of the shape to make sits in the middle of the table and is the largest thing on screen; the pieces are dragged onto it. Above the table, 4 outline cards sit in a row: a slanted parallelogram, a rectangle twice as long as it is tall, a triangle with a right angle at the top, and a four-sided shape with a short top and a long bottom. Tap a card to bring its outline to the middle. Controls: drag a piece to move it; Turn turns the chosen piece one step at a time; Flip flips the chosen piece over; a piece snaps to a side or a corner of the outline when it is close, with a soft click; tap a piece to show its name label (for example large triangle); Check looks at the outline. Two sorting trays labelled 3 sides and 4 sides appear on the sorting card. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Hint, Retry (clears the outline), Reset (returns all the pieces to the tray), Undo, Back and Next are in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the name label of the chosen piece, the number of pieces in the outline (for example pieces in the outline: 3), a message line that says what Check found, and the card number out of 5.
feedback: A piece brought close to a side or a corner of the outline snaps in with a soft click. Pieces that overlap each other or stick out of the outline glow soft amber with the note: These pieces overlap. Move one piece.

Check says what it sees. A full outline gets: The outline is full with no gap and no overlap. A gap glows amber with a clue, for example: A gap is left near the top corner. Which piece has a corner that fits it?

After an outline is filled the tool says: These pieces fit the shape: more than one way is allowed. It then invites the student to press Retry and fill the same outline with a different set of pieces.

On the sorting card a piece dropped in the wrong tray slides back with the clue: Count the sides of this piece. A name label that does not fit the piece shows the amber note: Look at the size and at the number of sides.
A wrong answer shows a soft amber note and never a red cross; the tool names the piece it expected only after the second try.
tool_config.done_when: All 7 pieces are sorted and named, a square is made from 2 small triangles, the triangle outline is filled in 2 different ways, and all 4 outlines from the book are filled.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1: sort the 7 pieces into the trays 3 sides and 4 sides, and tap each piece to read its name. Answer: 3 sides: 2 large triangles, 1 medium triangle and 2 small triangles (5 pieces). 4 sides: the square and the parallelogram (2 pieces). 5 + 2 = 7 pieces.
Card 2: make a square from 2 small triangles. Answer: join the 2 small triangles along their longest sides. They make a square the same size as the tangram square.
Card 3: fill the triangle outline (a right angle at the top) with 1 piece. Answer: the medium triangle fills it, with its longest side at the bottom.

Card 4: clear the triangle outline and fill it again with 2 pieces. Answer: the 2 small triangles fill it, side by side with their right angles together at the middle of the bottom. A shape can be made in more than one way.

Challenge: 'Now, use some or all of the pieces of your tangram set to make the following shapes. There may be more than one way to do it.' Fill all 4 outlines. Answer: one way for each, and yours may differ. The rectangle: the medium triangle in the middle with its longest side at the bottom and a small triangle in the gap on each side. The slanted parallelogram: the medium triangle on the left and the 2 small triangles together on the right. The triangle: the medium triangle. The four-sided shape with a short top and a long bottom: the parallelogram on the left and the medium triangle on the right, with the longest side of the medium triangle at the bottom. The rectangle can also be made from the square and the 2 small triangles.

hint_ladder.text: Look at the biggest corner of the outline: which piece has a corner like it?
Place the largest piece that fits first, then fill the gaps that are left with smaller pieces. Turn or flip a piece if it does not fit.
For the rectangle, lay the longest side of the medium triangle along the bottom. A small triangle fits the gap on each side.
The tool places one piece in the outline for you, and then a similar card follows.

media.instructions_for_student: The student names the seven tangram pieces, says how they are the same or different by sides and angles, and fills outlines with them in more than one way.
media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Tangram Maker
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S16.T16.C80.2D1
- Tool type: Puzzle (name the pieces, compare them, fill outlines)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Tangram: the seven-piece tangram set, the questions on naming the pieces and on how their angles and sides are the same or different, and the four outlines to make (a slanted parallelogram, a rectangle, a triangle and a four-sided shape with a short top and a long bottom) (developer only). Piece sizes in units where a small triangle has legs of 1: small triangles legs 1; medium triangle legs 1.41 (longest side 2); large triangles legs 2; square side 1; parallelogram sides 1 and 1.41.
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student names the seven tangram pieces, says how they are the same or different by their sides and angles, and makes shapes from some or all of the pieces in more than one way.
- Out of scope: measuring angles, how much space a piece covers, tangram pictures of animals or people.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A dark walnut tangram box seen from above, open, with the 7 flat coloured pieces in it: 2 large triangles (lavender and yellow), 1 medium triangle (orange), 2 small triangles (green and light blue), a square (pink) and a parallelogram (purple). On a cream card in the middle of the table lies the black outline of a triangle with a right angle at the top, the largest thing on the stage (base 140 pixels when a small-triangle leg is 70).
- Instruction line: "Make a square from the 2 small triangles."
- The two small triangles pulse once.
2. Scene and Objects
- Pieces: flat with a soft shadow and thin white edges; a name tag shows when a piece is tapped (for example "large triangle").
- Outline cards: a row of 4 small cards above the table: a slanted parallelogram (base 2, height 1, slanted corners), a rectangle 2 long and 1 high, a triangle with a right angle at the top (base 2, height 1) and a four-sided shape with a short top (1), a long bottom (3) and height 1. Tap a card to bring its outline to the middle.
- Corner tester: a small wooden card with a right angle. Side check: tap two sides of a piece to lay one on the other.
- Read-outs: the name of the chosen piece, "pieces in the outline: 3", and a line saying what the tool found. Goal chip on the table. Bottom buttons (large, three only): Hint, Reset, Next. Next is locked until the goal chip is green.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a piece; it snaps to a side or a corner of an outline or another piece when close. A round "Turn" handle turns the chosen piece one step (an eighth of a full turn); a round "Flip" handle flips it over.
- The tool checks the outline after every move: it is full when the pieces lie inside it with no gap and no overlap. Reset returns all pieces to the box.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Make a square from the 2 small triangles." Goal chip: "Make a square". Setup: the 2 small triangles and the pink square beside them. Help: guided, the long side of each small triangle glows. Guess: "Which sides will touch?" with cards "the long sides" and "the short sides". Result: joined along their long sides they make a square exactly the size of the tangram square; the pink square lies over it and matches. Why line: "2 small triangles joined along their long sides make a square the same size as the tangram square."
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Fill the triangle outline with 1 piece." Goal chip: "1 piece". Setup: the triangle outline. Help: guided, name tags shown. Guess: "Which piece will fill it?" with cards "a small triangle", "the medium triangle" and "a large triangle". Result: the medium triangle fits, its longest side along the bottom. Why line: "The medium triangle fills the outline: its longest side lies along the bottom."
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Now fill the same outline with 2 pieces." Goal chip: "2 pieces". Setup: the same outline, cleared. Guess: "Which 2 pieces will fill it?" cards "2 small triangles", "a small triangle and a square" and "2 large triangles". Result: the 2 small triangles fill it, side by side with their right angles together at the middle of the bottom. Why line: "The same shape can be made in more than one way: 1 medium triangle, or 2 small triangles." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Fill a large triangle with the medium triangle and the 2 small triangles." Goal chip: "3 pieces". Setup: the outline of a large triangle (legs 2). Guess: "How many pieces will you need?" cards 2, 3 and 4. Result: the medium triangle and the 2 small triangles fill it. Why line: "2 small triangles make a triangle as big as the medium one, and 2 medium-size triangles fill a large triangle: 1 + 2 = 3 pieces." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "Look at the tangram set. Cut out all the shapes. Name them." Goal chip: "Name 7 pieces". Setup: the 7 pieces and 5 name tags: "large triangle", "medium triangle", "small triangle", "square" and "parallelogram". Guess: "How many of the 7 pieces are triangles?" cards 3, 5 and 7. The child drags a tag onto each piece. Result: 2 large triangles, 1 medium triangle, 2 small triangles, 1 square and 1 parallelogram. Why line: "2 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 = 7 pieces." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 2. Goal line: "How are they same or different from each other?" Goal chip: "Same or different". Setup: 6 statement cards. Guess: "Are all 7 pieces the same size?" cards "Yes" and "No". The child lays pieces on each other to check, then taps the true cards: "All have straight sides and corners", "The 5 triangles have the same shape", "The pieces come in different sizes" and "The square and the parallelogram have 4 sides, the triangles have 3". The false cards, "All pieces have 3 sides" and "All pieces are the same size", slide back. Result: the 4 true cards turn green. Why line: "Same: straight sides, and the 5 triangles are one shape. Different: the sizes, and 3 sides or 4." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 3. Goal line: "What do you notice about the angles of each of the shapes?" Goal chip: "Angles". Setup: the corner tester. Guess: "How many right angles does a triangle have?" cards 0, 1, 2 and 3. The child lays the tester on every corner of one triangle, the square and the parallelogram. Result: each triangle has 1 right angle and 2 equal angles, the square has 4 right angles, the parallelogram has no right angle and its opposite angles are equal. Why line: "A triangle folded through its right angle has its other 2 corners land on each other, so they are equal." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 4. Goal line: "What do you notice about the sides of each of the shapes?" Goal chip: "Sides". Guess: "How many sides of a triangle are equal?" cards 0, 2 and 3. The child taps two sides of a piece to lay them on each other. Result: each triangle has 2 equal sides and a longer third side, the square has 4 equal sides, the parallelogram has equal opposite sides in 2 different lengths. Why line: "Sides that lie exactly on each other are equal." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 5. Goal line: "Now, use some or all of the pieces of your tangram set to make the following shapes. There may be more than one way to do it." Goal chip: "4 shapes". Setup: the 4 outline cards. Guess: before each outline, the number of pieces to use (cards 2, 3 and 4). The child fills all 4. Result: for example the rectangle from the medium triangle with a small triangle on each side, the slanted parallelogram from the medium triangle and the 2 small triangles side by side, the triangle from the medium triangle, and the four-sided shape from the parallelogram and the medium triangle; the rectangle can also be made from the square and the 2 small triangles. Why line: "Each outline is full with no gap and no overlap, and there is more than one way." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- The pieces are 5 triangles of three sizes and 2 four-sided pieces; every triangle has a right angle and 2 equal sides; pieces can swap places to fill the same outline.
- Rules in the child's words: "Name a piece by its sides and size." "Every triangle in the set has a right angle and 2 equal sides." "A shape can often be made in more than one way."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Wrong answer: red strip, a small shake of the object, and one friendly line naming the mistake and what to look at. No scores; trying again is always free. Correct: the outline turns green, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks.
- Pieces overlap -> "These pieces overlap. Move one piece." The overlap glows orange.
- A gap is left -> "A gap is left near the top corner. Which piece has a corner that fits it?" The gap glows orange.
- Wrong name tag -> "Look at the size and at the number of sides." The piece's sides pulse.
- Joins the short sides to make a square -> "A square needs the long sides together." The long sides glow.
- Says every piece is the same size -> "Lay the small triangle on the large one. Do they match?" The two pieces slide together.
- Says the parallelogram has a right angle -> "Lay the corner tester on each corner of the parallelogram." The tester slides to the first corner.
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "Look at the biggest corner of the outline: which piece has a corner like it?" (2) Visual clue: a faint ghost of the largest piece that fits appears in the outline. (3) Almost the answer: the tool places one piece in the outline.
- Edge cases: the parallelogram needs Flip to fit some outlines; a piece lying half outside the outline is flagged until it is moved.
7. Ending
- A star challenge is done when its result in section 4 is reached; the end screen follows when all chips are green.
- End screen: confetti once. "Well done!" Remember: "The tangram has 5 triangles and 2 four-sided pieces." "Every triangle in the set has a right angle and 2 equal sides." "A shape can be made in more than one way." Think and talk: "Can you make the same rectangle with different pieces?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: dark walnut tangram box (photo); 7 tangram pieces as flat coloured cut-outs; cream outline card; wooden corner tester (photo cut-out). Name tags and cards are code-drawn. No people. English only.

media.teaching_notes: 1. Use some or all of the 7 pieces. The pieces must not overlap, and they must fill the outline with no gap. 2. Rectangle: put the medium triangle in the middle with its longest side at the bottom. Put a small triangle in the gap on each side. The 3 pieces fill the rectangle. 3. Slanted parallelogram: put the medium triangle on the left. Put the 2 small triangles together on the right, so that they make a second triangle the size of the medium one. The 2 triangles side by side make the slanted shape. 4. Triangle: the medium triangle fills it, with its longest side at the bottom. The 2 small triangles also fill it, side by side with their right angles together at the middle of the bottom. 5. Four-sided shape with a short top and a long bottom: put the parallelogram on the left and the medium triangle on the right, with the longest side of the medium triangle at the bottom. 6. More than one way: the rectangle can also be made from the square and the 2 small triangles, and the parallelogram from the square with a small triangle on each side. 7. Check: each outline is filled with no gap and no overlap. Answer: Sample answer: rectangle and parallelogram: medium triangle and 2 small triangles. Triangle: medium triangle. content.text:

2. The $5$ triangles have the same shape in $3$ sizes: the $2$ small triangles are the same size, the $2$ large triangles are the same size, and the medium triangle is in between.

Answer: Same: all have straight sides, and the $5$ triangles have the same shape. Different: the sizes differ, and the square and parallelogram have $4$ sides, not $3$.
[Image: Tangram: Ans2: solution (continued)]

content.text:
1. Look at the $5$ triangles. Each triangle has $1$ right angle and $2$ equal angles.
2. Look at the square. All $4$ angles are right angles, so all $4$ are equal.
3. Look at the parallelogram. It has no right angle, and its opposite angles are equal.
[Image: Tangram: Ans3: solution]
4. Check: fold a triangle in half through its right angle. The other $2$ corners land on each other, so those $2$ angles are equal.
Answer: Each triangle has $1$ right angle and $2$ equal angles. The square has $4$ right angles. The parallelogram has no right angle, and its opposite angles are equal.
[Image: Tangram: Ans3: solution (continued)]

content.text:
1. Look at the $5$ triangles. Each triangle has $2$ equal sides, and its third side is longer.
2. Look at the square. All $4$ sides are equal.
3. Look at the parallelogram. Its opposite sides are equal, and it has $2$ different lengths: $2$ longer sides and $2$ shorter sides.
4. Check: lay pieces edge to edge to compare the sides. Equal sides match exactly.
Answer: Each triangle has $2$ equal sides. The square has $4$ equal sides. The parallelogram has equal opposite sides, in $2$ different lengths.

content.text: Now, use some or all of the pieces of your tangram set to make the following shapes. There may be more than one way to do it.

content.question: Now, use some or all of the pieces of your tangram set to make the following shapes. There may be more than one way to do it.

content.question_tex: Now, use some or all of the pieces of your tangram set to make the following shapes. There may be more than one way to do it.
content.publication_text: Now, use some or all of the pieces of your tangram set to make the following shapes. There may be more than one way to do it.

content.text:
1. Use some or all of the $7$ pieces. The pieces must not overlap, and they must fill the outline with no gap.
2. Rectangle: put the medium triangle in the middle with its longest side at the bottom. Put a small triangle in the gap on each side. The $3$ pieces fill the rectangle.
[Image: Tangram: Ans5: solution]
3. Slanted parallelogram: put the medium triangle on the left. Put the $2$ small triangles together on the right, so that they make a second triangle the size of the medium one. The $2$ triangles side by side make the slanted shape.
4. Triangle: the medium triangle fills it, with its longest side at the bottom. The $2$ small triangles also fill it, side by side with their right angles together at the middle of the bottom.
5. Four-sided shape with a short top and a long bottom: put the parallelogram on the left and the medium triangle on the right, with the longest side of the medium triangle at the bottom.
6. More than one way: the rectangle can also be made from the square and the $2$ small triangles, and the parallelogram from the square with a small triangle on each side.
7. Check: each outline is filled with no gap and no overlap.
Answer: Sample answer: rectangle and parallelogram: medium triangle and $2$ small triangles. Triangle: medium triangle. Last shape: parallelogram and medium triangle. Your answer may differ.
[Image: Tangram: Ans5: solution (continued)]

media.title: Shape Detective

tool_config.idea: Drag the corners of one four-sided shape and switch two locks to see when it is a square, a rectangle, a rhombus or a parallelogram, then test seven statements about sides and angles and see that one statement can fit more than one shape.
tool_config.title: Shape Detective
tool_config.screen: The detective's board on the craft table, drawn as a warm 3-D isometric scene with soft shadows and gentle animation. A pinboard in the middle holds one four-sided shape on a dot grid, and it is the largest thing on screen. The shape has four round corner handles that can be dragged. Its four sides show their lengths in centimetres next to them (practice values), and every corner that is a right angle carries a small square mark. To the left of the board are two locks: a Sides lock with three positions, Off, Opposite sides equal and All sides equal, and an Angles lock with two positions, Off and Right angles. A name plate above the shape reads Four-sided shape, Parallelogram, Rhombus, Rectangle or Square, whichever fits the shape now. Along the bottom lies a shelf of seven statement cards numbered 1 to 7 with the book's wording, and on the right are four shape cards: Square, Rectangle, Rhombus and Parallelogram. An instruction strip at the top shows one sentence in large type, with progress dots under it. Controls: drag a corner handle (the locks decide what the other corners do, so the sides or angles stay as set); switch each lock; drag a statement card onto the shape to test it, or onto a shape card to match it; Check, Hint, Undo, Retry (clears the last match), Reset (clears all matches and unlocks the shape), Back and Next in the same places on every card. Read-outs: the four side lengths, the right angle marks, the name plate, a tester light on each statement card that shows fits in green or look again in soft amber with the reason, and a match tally that counts how many statements are matched to each shape (for example Rhombus: 3).
feedback: A statement card dropped on a shape shows a green tester light when it fits and a soft amber light when it does not, with the reason, for example: Statement 7 fits the rectangle: its opposite angles are equal and its sides make right angles.
When a lock is set the shape keeps what the lock says while you drag. Under Opposite sides equal the other corners follow, so the opposite sides stay equal, and the name plate changes at once.
A rectangle also has opposite angles equal: statement 7 fits it too, so the tool says that one statement can fit more than one shape.
Statement 1 dropped on the square shows soft amber: all my angles are right angles is true for the square, but its sides are all equal, so all my sides are not equal does not fit.

A wrong match slides back with a clue such as: Check the sides first. Are all four equal? It never shows a red mark. A shape card that has a match gets a small green tick and the tally counts it, for example: Statement 3 fits 2 shapes.
tool_config.done_when: All four shapes have been made with the locks, statements have been tested on them, all seven statements are matched, and the student has said which statements fit more than one shape.

placement.where: last concept of the topic, after its teaching and worked examples

challenges: Card 1: set the Sides lock to All sides equal and the Angles lock to Right angles, then drag a corner. What shape is it, and what happens to the sides when you drag? Answer: a square. The four sides grow or shrink together and stay equal, and the four angles stay right angles.

Card 2: set the Sides lock to Opposite sides equal and the Angles lock to Right angles, then drag a corner. Which shape is it? Answer: a rectangle. Opposite sides stay equal, the four angles stay right angles, and the sides next to each other can be different.

Card 3: set the Sides lock to All sides equal and the Angles lock to Off, then drag a corner until no angle is a right angle. Which shape is it? Answer: a rhombus. All four sides are equal and the angles are not right angles.

Card 4: set the Sides lock to Opposite sides equal and the Angles lock to Off, then drag a corner so that the sides next to each other are different and no angle is a right angle. Which shape is it? Answer: a parallelogram. Opposite sides are equal and the angles are not right angles.

Card 5: make each of your four shapes in turn and drag statement 6, 'My opposite angles are equal and so are my sides.', onto it. On which shapes does it fit? Answer: on all four, because each of them has opposite sides equal and opposite angles equal.

Challenge: 'Match the statements with appropriate shapes. Do some of them describe more than one shape?' The statements are 1: All my angles are right angles, but all my sides are not equal. 2: All my sides are equal, but all my angles are not. 3: My opposite angles are equal, but my sides do not make a right angle. 4: Two pairs of sides are equal, but they do not make a right angle. 5: All my sides make right angles with each other and are equal. 6: My opposite angles are equal and so are my sides. 7: My opposite angles are equal and my sides make right angles. The shapes are Square, Rectangle, Rhombus and Parallelogram. Answer: 1 Rectangle; 2 Rhombus; 3 Rhombus and Parallelogram; 4 Parallelogram and Rhombus; 5 Square; 6 all four shapes; 7 Square and Rectangle. Yes, statements 3, 4, 6 and 7 describe more than one shape.

Statement 5 says all sides equal and all angles right angles. Set All sides equal and Right angles and the name plate says Square. The tool then matches statement 5 with Square so you can see how a match is made.

media.description:
A. TOOL TITLE
- Shape Detective
B. TOOL INFO
- Tool ID: M3.S18.T18.C92.2D1
- Tool type: Puzzle (make four-sided shapes with two locks, then match statements to shapes)
- Textbook source: Shapes and Patterns, Which Shape Am I?: the table of seven statements and the shapes Square, Rectangle, Rhombus and Parallelogram (developer only). Practice values: a first rectangle 10 cm by 3 cm, the statements "All my sides are equal" and "I have 4 right angles".
C. LEARNING OBJECTIVE
- The student tells a square, a rectangle, a rhombus and a parallelogram apart by checking the sides and then the angles, and sees that one statement can describe more than one shape.
- Out of scope: kites, measuring angles, and any shape with more than 4 sides.
D. TOOL DESCRIPTION
1. Opening Screen
- A detective's cork pinboard seen from above. In the middle, a red string is stretched round four brass pins and makes a rectangle (10 cm by 3 cm, with a small square mark at each right angle). It is the largest thing on the stage. Above the shape two brass dial locks sit side by side, "Sides" and "Angles", next to a brass name plate that reads "Rectangle". Four cards with outlines are pinned in a row along the bottom of the board: a green square, a purple rectangle, a blue rhombus (a slanted shape with equal sides) and a yellow parallelogram. Seven index cards numbered 1 to 7 lie on a shelf under the board.
- Instruction line: "Set both locks to make a square."
- The Sides lock pulses once.
2. Scene and Objects
- Shape: 4 round brass pins are the corners; the side lengths show next to each side in whole cm; a small square mark sits on every right angle.
- Sides lock, 3 positions: "Off", "Opposite sides equal" and "All sides equal". Angles lock, 2 positions: "Off" and "Right angles". The two locks decide what the other pins do when one pin is dragged.
- Name plate: "Four-sided shape", "Parallelogram", "Rhombus", "Rectangle" or "Square", always the most special name that fits.
- Index cards 1 to 7 carry the statements, in full, with the wording of the question. A small tester light sits on each card: green when it fits the shape on the board, orange with a reason when it does not.
- Shape cards: 4 pinned cards, each with a small tick box. A tally under each card counts the statements matched, for example "Rhombus: 3".
- Goal chip, for example "Make a square". Bottom buttons (large, three only): Hint, Reset, Next. Next is locked until the goal chip is green.
3. Main Interaction
- Drag a pin. With both locks Off the pins move one by one. With "Opposite sides equal" and Angles Off, the pin across from the dragged pin moves the other way, so the shape stays a parallelogram. With "All sides equal" and Angles Off, the other two pins turn too, so all 4 sides stay equal (a rhombus). With "Right angles" the shape stays a rectangle, or a square when "All sides equal" is also on.
- Turn a lock by tapping it. When a lock is changed, the shape rebuilds itself as the nearest shape of that kind (for example from a rectangle 10 by 3 to a square with sides of 10).
- Drag an index card onto the board to test it on the shape there, or onto a shape card to match it with that shape. A match is kept only if the statement is true for that shape; otherwise the card slides back with a clue.
- Reset clears the matches and unlocks both locks.
4. Activities
- Activity 1 (guided). Goal line: "Set both locks to make a square." Goal chip: "Make a square". Setup: the rectangle 10 by 3. Help: guided, each lock position shows a small label. Guess: "What will the name plate say?" with cards "Square", "Rectangle" and "Rhombus". Result: Sides lock "All sides equal" and Angles lock "Right angles"; the child drags a pin and the 4 sides grow and shrink together. Why line: "All 4 sides are equal and all 4 angles are right angles: a square."
- Activity 2 (guided). Goal line: "Now make a rectangle." Goal chip: "Make a rectangle". Help: guided. Guess: cards "Square", "Rectangle" and "Parallelogram" for the name plate with Sides lock "Opposite sides equal" and Angles lock "Right angles". Result: the child drags a pin; opposite sides stay equal and the 4 angles stay right angles, while sides next to each other can be different. Why line: "Opposite sides are equal and all 4 angles are right angles: a rectangle."
- Activity 3 (independent). Goal line: "Make a shape with all sides equal and no right angle." Goal chip: "Make a rhombus". Setup: locks free. Guess: cards "Square", "Rhombus" and "Parallelogram". Result: Sides lock "All sides equal", Angles lock "Off"; the child drags a pin until no angle is a right angle (the shape is slanted). Why line: "All 4 sides are equal and the angles are not right angles: a rhombus." Help: independent.
- Activity 4 (independent). Goal line: "Make a shape with opposite sides equal, sides next to each other different, and no right angle." Goal chip: "Make a parallelogram". Guess: cards "Rectangle", "Rhombus" and "Parallelogram". Result: Sides lock "Opposite sides equal", Angles lock "Off"; the child drags a pin until two sides next to each other have different lengths and no angle is right. Why line: "Opposite sides are equal and the angles are not right angles: a parallelogram." Help: independent.
- Activity 5 (independent). Goal line: "Make each of your 4 shapes. Test the card 'All my sides are equal' on each one." Goal chip: "Test a card". Setup: a practice card "All my sides are equal" lies on the board. Guess: "On how many of the 4 shapes will it fit?" with cards 1, 2, 3 and 4. Result: it fits the square and the rhombus. Why line: "All sides equal is true for the square and the rhombus. In the rectangle and the parallelogram the sides next to each other can be different." Help: independent.
- Star Challenge 1. Goal line: "Match the statements with appropriate shapes. Do some of them describe more than one shape? (1) All my angles are right angles, but all my sides are not equal. (2) All my sides are equal, but all my angles are not. (3) My opposite angles are equal, but my sides do not make a right angle. (4) Two pairs of sides are equal, but they do not make a right angle. (5) All my sides make right angles with each other and are equal. (6) My opposite angles are equal and so are my sides. (7) My opposite angles are equal and my sides make right angles." Goal chip: "Match 7 statements". Guess: "How many of the 7 statements describe more than one shape?" with cards 2, 4 and 6. The child tests each statement on the board (using the locks) and matches it with every shape it fits. Truth table the tool uses: 1 Rectangle; 2 Rhombus; 3 Rhombus and Parallelogram; 4 Parallelogram and Rhombus; 5 Square; 6 Square, Rectangle, Rhombus and Parallelogram; 7 Square and Rectangle. The goal is done when all 13 matches are kept. Result: the tally reads Square: 3, Rectangle: 3, Rhombus: 4, Parallelogram: 3, and the line says "Statements 3, 4, 6 and 7 describe more than one shape." Why line: "A rhombus, a rectangle and a square all have opposite sides equal, so statement 6 fits all four shapes: 3 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 13 matches." Help: independent.
5. Mathematical Understanding
- Dragging pins with the locks on, the child sees that two questions sort the four shapes: are all sides equal, and are all angles right angles. A shape can fit a statement and still be called by a more special name, so one statement can fit several shapes.
- Rules in the child's words: "Check the sides, then the angles." "All sides equal and right angles: square. Opposite sides equal and right angles: rectangle. All sides equal and no right angle: rhombus. Opposite sides equal and no right angle: parallelogram." "One statement can fit more than one shape."
6. Feedback and Hints
- Every wrong answer: the feedback strip turns red, the object shakes a little, and one friendly line names the mistake and what to look at. No scores; trying again is always free.
- Correct: the tester light and the matched card turn green, the goal chip turns green with a gentle bounce, the pill gets a tick and Next unlocks.
- Matches statement 1 with the square -> "Statement 1 says the sides are not all equal, but a square has 4 equal sides." The 4 sides of the square pulse.
- Matches statement 2 with the square -> "Statement 2 says the angles are not all right angles, but a square has 4 right angles." The 4 right angle marks pulse.
- Matches statement 6 with only the parallelogram -> "A rectangle, a rhombus and a square also have opposite sides equal and opposite angles equal. Try them on the board." The other 3 shape cards pulse.
- Says a rectangle is not a parallelogram -> "A rectangle has opposite sides equal too. Test statement 6 on it." The rectangle card pulses.
- Names a shape from the sides only -> "Check the sides first. Are all four equal? Then check the angles." The two locks pulse in turn.
- Hint button, 3 levels. (1) Words: "Read the statement slowly. What does it say about the sides, and what does it say about the angles?" (2) Visual clue: the board shows the shape for the statement and the tester light. (3) Almost the answer: "Statement 5 says all sides equal and all angles right angles: the name plate says Square", and the tool matches statement 5 with the square.
- Edge cases: a rhombus dragged until its angles are right angles becomes a square, and the name plate changes at once; a rectangle dragged until all its sides are equal becomes a square; with Sides lock on "All sides equal" the side lengths always show the same number.
7. Ending
- A star challenge is done when its result in section 4 is reached; the end screen follows when all chips are green.
- End screen: confetti once. "Well done!" Remember: "Check the sides, then the angles." "A rectangle is a parallelogram with 4 right angles." "One statement can fit more than one shape." Think and talk: "Which statement from the table fits all four shapes?" Button: "Start again".
8. Assets and Language
- Images: cork pinboard (photo); brass pins and brass dial locks (photo cut-outs); red string (photo-style line); wooden-framed index cards (photo-style); 4 pinned shape cards (flat outlines in green, purple, blue and yellow). The name plate is a brass plate (photo cut-out) with code-drawn letters. No people. English only.
