objectives.objective_text: Students describe one row of a weave in words by counting the over and under steps and saying repeat, and write the next row by swapping over and under.
Students write the rows of a weave until a row is the same as Row 1, and say after how many rows the pattern repeats.
Students build rows of a weave from rules of over and under steps, and find the row where the pattern starts to repeat.
Students sort shapes into regular and not regular by comparing the lengths of their sides, and name a regular pentagon and a regular octagon.
Students decide whether copies of a shape fill the space round a point with no gap and no overlap, and say that such a shape tessellates.
Students fit regular triangles, squares, pentagons, hexagons and octagons around a point and say which fit with no gap and no overlap.
Students list the shapes that meet at the joins of a border made of two shapes that take turns, and say whether the same set of shapes meets at every join.
Students continue a pattern made of two shapes on a dot grid, and list the shapes that meet at a marked point.
Students name an isosceles triangle by its 2 equal sides, and fold it in half to show that it also has 2 equal angles.
Students name a triangle as equilateral, isosceles or scalene from the lengths of its sides, and say how many of its angles are equal.
Students make triangles from the pieces of a rhombus, measure their sides and fold them, and say whether each triangle is equilateral, isosceles or scalene.
Students tell a kite from a parallelogram by checking whether the equal sides are next to each other or opposite each other.
Students name a four-sided shape with equal opposite sides as a parallelogram, and tell a rectangle from other parallelograms by its right angles.
Students join 2, 3 and 4 pieces of the rhombus side to side, count the sides of each shape made, and name the four-sided shapes by their sides and angles.
Students sort the 7 tangram pieces by their number of sides, and name each piece as a small, medium or large triangle, a square or a parallelogram.
Students name the seven tangram pieces, say how they are the same or different, and make shapes from some or all of the pieces in more than one way.
Students name a four-sided shape as a square, rectangle, rhombus or parallelogram by checking its sides and its angles, and say which statements fit more than one of these shapes.
Students match seven statements about sides and angles with the square, rectangle, rhombus or parallelogram they describe, and find which statements fit more than one shape.
Students join the ends of two diameters of a circle and name the shape formed by checking its sides and its angles.
Students join points round a circle by a repeating move, such as on by 4 and back by 3, and count the lines when the thread is back at the start.
Students draw two diameters of a circle, join the ends and check the shape, and thread the points of a circle to make a string design.
Students use two views of a cube to name the face opposite a given face and say which clue they used.
Students sort the small cubes of a big painted cube into corners, edges, face middles and inside, and count how many have three, two, one or no painted faces.
Students find opposite faces of a cube, place pictures on a net, and count painted and removed small cubes in a cube frame and in a painted cube.
Students place five shapes in a line by using each clue in turn, starting with the surest clue, and check every clue against the finished line.
Students place seven shapes in a line by using five clues one at a time, and check every clue against the finished line.
Students count the faces and vertices of a solid by ticking each one once, and say how many faces meet at a vertex.
Students count the edges of a solid by adding the sides of all its faces and halving the total, because each edge is the side of two faces.
Students count the faces, vertices and edges of each solid, the icosahedron and the dodecahedron, and say how many faces meet at each vertex.

video_coverage.book_item: Book item: Can you figure out how to make this mat? Let us try to understand how this mat is woven by looking at the pattern in the first two rows. Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... Row 2: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, 1 over, ... You can use strips of the same colour or 2 different colours, one for each row.

Book item: Try to weave a pattern, using the rules given below. Row 1: 2 over, 1 under, 2 over, 1 under, ... (repeat). Row 2: 1 under (do not repeat), 3 over, 3 under, 3 over, 3 under, ... (repeat). Row 3: 2 under, 1 over, 2 under, ... (repeat). Row 4: 1 over (do not repeat), 3 under, 3 over, ... (repeat). Continue weaving in this order.
Book item: Can you work out the steps for any of these designs and weave the pattern? Write the steps of the pattern in your notebook for each row until it starts repeating.
Book item: Draw the following pattern on a grid paper. Part of it is done for you. Now, complete the rest of the grid to get the full design.
Book item: We have placed 3 pentagons around a point. Can we fit one more into the empty space?
Book item: Can regular triangles fit together at a point without any gap? How many of them fit together?
Book item: Can squares (a regular 4-sided shape) fit together around a point without any gap or overlap? Try it out using cutouts of squares. How many squares did you need?
Book item: Can five squares fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Why or why not?
Book item: Can regular hexagons (6-sided shapes with equal sides) fit together around a point without any gaps or overlaps? Try and see. How many fit together at a point?
Book item: Do regular octagons fit together without any gaps or overlaps? Try drawing the same and check.
Book item: Here is a tessellating pattern with more than one shape. What shapes have been used in this pattern? ___, ___.
Book item: Continue the pattern given below and colour it appropriately.

Book item: Look at the pattern given below. What shapes are coming together at the marked points? Are the same set of shapes coming together at these points? Continue the pattern and colour it appropriately.
Book item: Here is a tiling pattern made using two different shapes, squares and triangles. Are the triangles equilateral? Why or why not?
Book item: What shapes are coming together at the marked points? Are the same set of shapes coming together at these points? Continue the pattern and colour it appropriately.
Book item: Create similar patterns using other cutouts of shapes.
Book item: What geometrical shapes can you make by fitting 2 of these triangles together? Trace the shapes you created.
Book item: How many different types of triangles can you make? Now, observe and measure the sides of these triangles. What do you notice?
Book item: Trace the isosceles triangles on a paper and cut them out. Fold them in half. What do you notice about their angles?
Book item: Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are equal (equilateral triangle)?
Book item: Is it possible to make a triangle where all three sides are unequal?
Book item: Take an equilateral triangle. Check if all the angles of an equilateral triangle are equal, just like you did with the isosceles triangle.
Book item: Now, cut the equilateral triangle in half. How many sides of each new triangle are equal?
Book item: Check in scalene triangles whether any two or more angles are equal?
Book item: How many different 4-sided shapes (quadrilaterals) can you make?
Book item: Measure the sides of each of these two quadrilaterals A and B. What do you notice? Are there any pairs of sides that are equal? Which pairs are equal, adjacent or opposite?
Book item: What types of angles do quadrilaterals A and B have? Which angles are equal in each of the above parallelograms?
Book item: In the grid given below, draw two different kites and parallelograms each.

Book item: Now, use 3 triangles from the rhombus to form shapes. How many sides do each one of them have? Using 3 triangular pieces of the rhombus, try creating: (a): a 3-sided shape; (b): a 4-sided shape; (c): a 5-sided shape.
Book item: Which of these shapes can be made with all 4 pieces? Try and find out. (a): Square; (b): Rectangle; (c): Triangle; (d): Pentagon, 5-sided; (e): Hexagon, 6-sided; (f): Octagon, 8-sided

Book item: Make your own kite shape. (a): Start with a square piece of paper. (b): Take one corner of the paper and fold it towards the opposite corner, creating a sharp crease along the diagonal. (c): Open and fold the corner A inwards, aligning the edge with the crease you just made. (d): Repeat on the other side, folding the other corner B inwards to align with the crease at the centre. You have a kite shape! What shapes do you see in the kite?
Book item: Look at the tangram set. Cut out all the shapes. Name them.
Book item: (a): How are they same or different from each other?
Book item: (b): What do you notice about the angles of each of the shapes?
Book item: (c): What do you notice about the sides of each of the shapes?
Book item: Now, use some or all of the pieces of your tangram set to make the following shapes. There may be more than one way to do it.

Book item: Match the statements with appropriate shapes. Do some of them describe more than one shape? (1): All my angles are right angles, but all my sides are not equal. (2): All my sides are equal, but all my angles are not. (3): My opposite angles are equal, but my sides do not make a right angle. (4): Two pairs of sides are equal, but they do not make a right angle. (5): All my sides make right angles with each other and are equal. (6): My opposite angles are equal and so are my sides. (7): My opposite angles are equal and my sides make right angles. The shapes: Square, Rectangle, Rhombus, Parallelogram.

Book item: (a): Draw a circle with a compass and mark its centre. (b): Draw its diameter. Mark the endpoints of the diameter. (c): Draw another diameter of the circle and mark the endpoints. (d): Now join the four points. What shape is formed? Check the sides of the quadrilateral and the angles obtained.
Book item: Try with a different pair of diameters. What do you notice about the shape that is formed?
Book item: Is it possible to create a 4-sided shape other than a rectangle through this process?
Book item: Look at the circle given below. It is marked with points 1 to 24. Join points 1 to 11, 11 to 2, 2 to 12, and so on till you reach back at 1.
Book item: Can you think of a way to make a design exactly like the image given here? Try to make it.
Book item: Here are three views of a cube. Can you draw them on the net in the correct order?
Book item: Here are some big solid cube frames. How many small cubes have been removed from each cube? (a), (b), (c)

Book item: Nisha has glued 27 small cubes together to make a large solid cube. She paints the large cube red. How many of the original small cubes have (a): three faces painted red? ___; (b): two faces painted red? ___; (c): one face painted red? ___; (d): no faces painted red? ___

Book item: Tanu arranged 7 shapes in a line. She used 2 squares, 2 triangles, 1 circle, 1 hexagon, and 1 rectangle. Find her arrangement using the following clues: (a): The square is between the circle and the rectangle. (b): The rectangle is between the square and the triangle. (c): The two triangles are next to the square. (d): The hexagon is to the right of the triangle. (e): The circle is to the left of the square.
Book item: What do these names mean? Once you count their faces, you will know.
Book item: What shapes do you see in an icosahedron and a dodecahedron? Icosahedron: ___ Dodecahedron: ___ Do all the faces look the same? Icosahedron: ___ Dodecahedron: ___
Book item: How many faces meet at a vertex (point)? Icosahedron: ___ Dodecahedron: ___ Do the same number of faces meet at each vertex? Icosahedron: ___ Dodecahedron: ___
Book item: How many edges do you see? Icosahedron: ___ Dodecahedron: ___ How did you count them such that you do not miss out any edge or count an edge twice?
Book item: Can you think of any other solid shapes that have faces that look the same? Do the same number of faces meet at each common vertex?
Book item: You can also build some solid shapes using straws or ice-cream sticks and clay or play dough. Which shapes did you make?

chapter_approach.intro: The chapter is a craft table: paper strips, tiles, cut-out pieces, thread and clay. Making and fitting shapes shows which shapes fit together, what makes a triangle or a four-sided shape what it is, and how patterns repeat. A short video explains each idea, and an interactive tool lets the student try it alone.

points.text: Every idea has one short concept video. The tool that follows is where the student weaves, fits, joins, folds and counts alone, with hints, retry and reset. Eleven tools, each with its own purpose, follow the chapter's own activities.
points.title: Videos teach, tools explore

points.text: Each tool opens with a short recall of the video idea, then lets the student play and apply it, and ends with the chapter's own question, used exactly as the book gives it.
points.title: A tool in three steps

points.text: Every answerable question and activity of the book is its own short video with a step by step solution and a question picture and a solution picture, in a Questions topic that follows the idea it practises.
points.title: Every book question has its own video

points.text: The book's cut-out pieces (the rhombus with four triangles, the tangram, the regular shapes, the nets) are shown on screen, so every student has a full set to turn, flip and join.
points.title: The pieces are on screen

points.text: The chapter compares angles by folding and by fitting pieces. It says right angle and equal angles and never measures an angle, and so does the plan.
points.title: No measuring of angles
